claims.claim: A credit score is a prediction of your credit behavior, such as how likely you are to pay a loan back on time, based on information from your credit reports.
A credit score is produced by a mathematical formula — called a scoring model — that turns the information in a credit report into a number.

The classic five factors in credit scoring are payment history, amounts owed, length of credit history, new credit, and credit mix; in FICO's classic model, payment history and amounts owed carry the most weight, and the importance of categories can vary from person to person.
Most credit scores in the common U.S. models range from roughly 300 to 850; the range is common rather than universal, and different models can use different ranges.
Usually a higher credit score makes it easier to qualify for a loan and may result in a better interest rate or loan terms; a higher score signals lower perceived risk.

A credit score is calculated from the information in credit reports; a credit report is the detailed record of credit activity — accounts, balances, and payment history — collected by credit reporting companies (bureaus) from creditors.
A person does not have just one credit score; the number can differ depending on the scoring model used, the source of the data, and even the day it was calculated.

Credit scores and credit reports are used by lenders deciding whether to offer mortgages, credit cards, auto loans, and other credit products, and by other businesses — landlords screening tenants, insurers, and companies providing cable, internet, utility, and cell phone service.

A credit score is a snapshot of the credit history at a point in time, not a permanent verdict: scores are recalculated as the underlying history changes, and lenders may also weigh factors beyond the score, such as income, employment history, and the kind of credit requested.

positions: CFI: 'A credit score ranges from 300 to 850.'
Some scoring models, including industry-specific scores, use other ranges.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states roughly 300 to 850 as the common range in major U.S. models and explicitly notes it is not universal, avoiding any claim that every score falls in this band.

positions: FICO publishes category weights of 35/30/15/10/10 for the general population.
FICO itself states the importance of these categories may vary from one person to another.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the classic five factors and says payment history and amounts owed carry the most weight in FICO's classic model, without presenting the percentages as universal rules.

positions: People commonly speak of 'the' credit score as if there were a single number.
CFPB: 'You do not have just one credit score' — it differs by model, data source, and even the day it is calculated.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the multiple-scores reality and frames any single number as one model's view of the same history.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The score's role in lending decisions
positions: Lenders use scores to help decide approval and terms.
FICO notes lenders may also look at income, how long the borrower has worked at their job, and the kind of credit requested.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson says the score summarizes the credit history, and that lenders look at more than the score, without overstating or understating its role.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no factual claims about credit scores; its boilerplate ('Credit Scores is a foundational concept in Personal Finance', 'a college-level explanation names the concept', 'label on a toolbox drawer') was discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generated boilerplate draft wholesale: the draft said nothing accurate about what a credit score is. The lesson is a fresh synthesis from CFPB, FICO, and CFI sources read live on 2026-08-21.
Avoided 'good credit' band labels (e.g., CFI's 'above 670') because thresholds vary by model and lender.
Did not adopt CFI's phrasing that scores are 'provided by' credit bureaus; the lesson follows CFPB/FICO, where a scoring model computes the score from bureau-held report data.

sourceRecords.title: What is a credit score? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Tier A. Supports: the working definition (a credit score is a prediction of credit behavior, such as how likely you are to pay a loan back on time, based on information from your credit reports); scoring models as mathematical formulas; the factor list (bill-paying history, current unpaid debt, number and type of loan accounts, how long accounts have been open, how much available credit is used, new applications, collections/foreclosure/bankruptcy recency); 'You do not have just one credit score'; 'Usually a higher score makes it easier to qualify for a loan and may result in a better interest rate or loan terms'; 'Most credit scores range from 300-850'; and users (mortgage, credit card, auto loan, tenant screening, insurance).

sourceRecords.title: What is a credit report? (Ask CFPB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Tier A. Supports: the credit report as a statement of credit activity (loan paying history and the status of credit accounts) collected by credit reporting companies from creditors; lenders using reports to decide whether to lend and at what interest rate; and non-lender users — insurers, landlords for rentals, and providers of cable TV, internet, utility, and cell phone service. Basis for the score-versus-report distinction in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: What's in my FICO Scores? — How are FICO Scores Calculated?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. The scoring company's own education page. Supports: the classic five categories — payment history (35%), amounts owed (30%), length of credit history (15%), new credit (10%), credit mix (10%) — with FICO's explicit caveat that category importance varies by person and score type; that FICO Scores are calculated only from credit report information; that credit reports and scores evolve frequently; and that lenders may also look at income, job tenure, and the kind of credit requested. The published percentages are reported in the lesson only as FICO's general weighting, not as universal.

sourceRecords.title: Credit Score — Definition, Users of Credit Scores, How to Improve
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Tier B secondary. Supports: the general definition (a number representing a borrower's credit standing, used to assess loan qualification and terms); the 300-850 range; and users (banks, credit card companies, fintech lenders, insurance companies, landlords, mortgage companies). CFI's 'respectable credit score above 670' band was deliberately NOT used — band labels vary by model and lender. CFI's phrasing that scores are 'provided by' credit bureaus was not adopted; the lesson follows CFPB/FICO, where a scoring model computes the score from bureau-held data.
